summary: Describes Time To Live handling in hierarchical MPLS networks, formalizing a TTL-transparent mode for a label-switched path. It specifies the Pipe and Uniform models for tunnels, with examples of pushing and popping labels, and updates RFC 3032.

eli5.summary: Packets carry a countdown so they cannot wander forever. This note says whether the tunnel counts each hop or hides them, so operators can choose.

subtitle: How the hop counter in an MPLS packet is handled when label-switched paths are stacked inside one another.

tldr.problem: RFC 3032 only covers the Uniform Model and says nothing about hierarchical LSPs, the Pipe Model or Penultimate Hop Popping, so TTL handling in tunnels was left undefined.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an incoming TTL (iTTL) and an outgoing TTL (oTTL) for every router and explains how they are set for Uniform, Short Pipe and Pipe Model LSPs, including push, swap, pop and PHP.
tldr.outcome: Operators can make a tunnel look like a single hop (Pipe) or show every router (Uniform). The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032 and has itself been updated by RFC 5462.

facts.label: Tunneled TTL drop over a Pipe LSP

today: RFC 3443 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003. It updates RFC 3032 and has itself been updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: Why TTL in MPLS Needed a Rewrite
sections.content:
RFC 3443 describes Time To Live (TTL) processing in hierarchical Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks. It was motivated by the need to formalize a TTL-transparent mode of operation for a label-switched path (LSP). It updates RFC 3032 (MPLS Label Stack Encoding) and complements RFC 3270 (MPLS Support of Differentiated Services).

The RFC lists three gaps in RFC 3032. It covers only the Uniform Model and does not address the Pipe Model or the Short Pipe Model. It does not cover hierarchical LSPs. And it does not define TTL processing in the presence of Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP).

The new Pipe Model supports the practice of configuring LSPs so that packets crossing the LSP see the tunnel as a single hop, however many label switch routers (LSRs) are inside it. The RFC says several vendors already provided this as an operator-configurable option.
sections.eli5: Old rules only said how to count when every stop on a trip is counted. People also wanted trips where the whole tunnel counts as one stop, so this note writes down both ways.

sections.title: Shim Header Fields and New Terms
sections.content:
An MPLS packet carries a shim header with four pieces of information: the MPLS label (20 bits), the TTL (8 bits), the bottom-of-stack flag (1 bit) and the experimental bits (3 bits). The experimental bits were later redefined in RFC 3270 to indicate scheduling and shaping behavior.

RFC 3443 adds three terms. iTTL is the TTL value to use as the incoming TTL, and no checks are performed on it. oTTL is the outgoing TTL, which is always iTTL - 1 unless stated otherwise. The oTTL check tests whether oTTL is greater than 0; if it is false, the packet is not forwarded. The check is only performed if an outgoing TTL (IP or MPLS) is set to oTTL.

The RFC splits TTL processing into two logical blocks: working out the incoming TTL, taking into account any tunnel exit caused by a Pop, and then processing the possibly exposed packet and its outgoing TTLs.

Signaling the LSP type (Pipe, Short Pipe or Uniform) is out of scope. LDP and RSVP-TE do not carry it, so the operator configures it manually, through a command line or a network management interface.
sections.eli5: Each router works out the countdown number that arrived, subtracts one, and throws the packet away if nothing is left. The tunnel type is chosen by a person, not announced by the network.

sections.title: The Uniform, Short Pipe and Pipe Models
sections.content:
In the Uniform Model, every node the LSP crosses is visible to nodes outside the tunnel. The inner and outer TTLs are synchronized at tunnel ingress and egress, so the tunnel behaves as if it were not there. This is consistent with RFC 3032 and applies with or without PHP.

In the Pipe Model, the MPLS network acts like a circuit and only the ingress and egress points are visible from outside. The outer TTL (N) may have no relationship to the tunneled TTL (n). The tunneled packet is decremented once on the way in and once at the egress, so its TTL ends at n-2. The RFC specifies the Pipe Model without PHP only.

The Short Pipe Model is a variation from RFC 3270 where the egress LSR bases its forwarding treatment on the tunneled packet rather than the encapsulating one. For TTL, it matches the Pipe Model without PHP. With PHP, the penultimate node pops the label and the egress node just decrements the header TTL. Either way, the tunneled packet's TTL has been decremented by two at the end of the LSP.
sections.eli5: Imagine a trip through a long hallway with a guard at every door. In the Uniform way, each guard stamps your card. In the Pipe way, you get one stamp going in and one coming out, and the doors inside are not counted.

sections.title: Computing iTTL and oTTL at Each Router
sections.content:
The incoming TTL depends on what arrives. For an IP packet, iTTL is the packet's TTL. For an MPLS packet that is being pushed, swapped or PHP-popped, iTTL is the TTL of the topmost incoming label.

When the router pops a label to end a tunnel, iTTL depends on the type of the LSP that was popped. For a Pipe Model LSP, iTTL is the TTL of the header exposed after the pop, which may be an IP header or another MPLS label. For a Uniform Model LSP, iTTL equals the TTL of the popped label. If several Pops happen in a row, the iTTL from the previous Pop replaces the TTL of each later label.

After iTTL, the oTTL check runs. If it passes, an IP-routed packet gets TTL oTTL (iTTL - 1). For packets routed as MPLS there are four cases: Swap-only sets the outgoing label's TTL to oTTL; Swap followed by Push does the swap the same way and sets pushed labels as in the next section; PHP pops the label; and a plain Pop happens before routing and is not considered here.

For PHP, the oTTL check is done regardless of whether oTTL is used. If the PHPed label belonged to a Short Pipe LSP, the exposed header's TTL is neither checked nor updated. If it belonged to a Uniform LSP, the exposed header's TTL is set to oTTL.
sections.eli5: When a packet arrives, the router first decides which countdown number to trust, then subtracts one. If the number would hit zero, the packet stops there.

sections.title: Pushing Labels at the Tunnel Entrance
sections.content:
At tunnel ingress, the TTL of each pushed label depends on the model. For each pushed Uniform Model label, the TTL is copied from the label or IP packet immediately underneath it. For each pushed Pipe Model or Short Pipe Model label, the TTL field is set to a value configured by the network operator. In most implementations, the default is 255.

This is why a Pipe tunnel hides its interior: the outer TTL starts from a fixed configured value and has no relationship to the tunneled packet's TTL, which is left untouched while the packet is inside.
sections.eli5: When a packet enters the tunnel, it gets a fresh outer ticket. In the Uniform way the ticket copies your number. In the Pipe way the ticket starts at a big preset number, usually 255.

sections.title: Implementation Remarks
sections.content:
The RFC adds three remarks for implementers. First, iTTL can be decremented by a value larger than 1 while it is being updated or oTTL is being determined, but this should only be used to compensate for network nodes that cannot decrement TTL values.

Second, whenever iTTL is decremented, the implementer must make sure the value does not become negative. Third, in the Short Pipe Model with PHP enabled, the TTL of the tunneled packet is unchanged after the PHP operation.
sections.eli5: Normally you take away exactly one. Never let the number go below zero, and do not take away more than one unless a router on the path cannot count for itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no new security issues beyond those in RFC 3032 and RFC 3270. It does not define a new protocol or expand an existing one. The authors believe that clarifying TTL handling in MPLS networks benefits service providers and their customers because troubleshooting is simplified.
sections.eli5: This note only explains how an existing counter works, so it brings no new dangers. Clear rules make problems easier to find.
